title: I can't code or draw, so I produced a full 190-card TCG with AI doing the work. It's free to play now. Here's how the producer + AI setup works.
author: Jumponturtles
selftext:
I'm one guy with a day job, no art budget and no coding background. Scuffle is mostly built by AI. My role is closer to a producer or creative director: the ideas, the rules, the world and the calls on what's fun are mine, and the AI turns them into a working game.



The game is a card game I invented, built on the old card game War: same suits and values, but every card has an ability. It has 190 cards, a story mode, PvP, ranked, Cups and trading. It's live and free to play in the browser right now.



Here's what that split actually looks like.



\*\*What I do\*\*



\- Design the game: the rules, all 190 cards, the factions, the story and characters, and the economy.

\- Give direction in plain words ("this card should feel sneaky", "ties go to War") and play everything to see if it's right.

\- Make the final call on anything creative: card text, art, prices and rewards.

\- Learn as I go. I'm picking up a lot of code just by reading what the AI writes and asking it to explain.



\*\*What the AI does\*\*



\- Writes all the code: the game engine, the website, the servers, the story mode and the Shop.

\- Generates every illustration in the game.

\- Builds its own tools: a test lab that runs huge batches of bot-vs-bot games so balance is based on real win rates, and a script that builds the card faces.



\*\*What made "producer + AI" actually work\*\*



\- \*\*Every decision gets written down.\*\* Each time I rule on something, it goes into a numbered decision log, and there are over a thousand entries now. Without it the AI forgets, contradicts itself, or "fixes" things I already decided. This was the single biggest lesson.

\- \*\*Separate AI chats with separate jobs\*\*, like a small studio: one writes and merges code, one runs testing, and side chats handle small assigned pieces. One clear job each stopped them stepping on each other.

\- \*\*Clear house rules for the AI.\*\* Only change what I asked for, ask when something's unclear, never delete anything without asking. Most of my early disasters came from the AI being "helpful" in ways I didn't ask for.



\*\*Art: the biggest hurdle by far\*\*



I'd love for all the art to be made by people eventually, but there's no budget, and the project couldn't happen any other way right now. What I learned:



\- \*\*Keep the AI away from the card layout.\*\* Whole-card generations gave a different frame every time and unreadable text. Now the AI makes only the illustration, and a normal script builds the card around it: the frame tinted with the suit color, the text panels in the faction color, the rarity mark, and text sized to fit. That's what finally made 190 cards look like one set.

\- \*\*One illustration, lots of assets.\*\* The same art becomes the Holo and Negative versions of a card, plus the matching sleeves, deck boxes, playmats and coins.

\- \*\*Characters are the hardest part.\*\* The story follows a winged green dinosaur and a goblin, and keeping them looking like the same characters across cards, story scenes and cosmetics took far more rerolls than anything else.



\*\*The honest part\*\*



This game would never have existed without AI. With a full-time job, a family and no money for programmers or artists, it was never going to get past a notebook. AI is the only reason there's a real, playable game instead of a "someday" idea.



I'm also honestly scared to post this. I've put a huge amount of my life into Scuffle: every card, every rule, every bit of the story and thousands of decisions. I know how a lot of people feel about AI games, and I'm afraid all of that work gets written off as "AI slop" before anyone actually plays it. I'm not trying to hide anything, which is why I'm laying out exactly how it was made. I just hope people judge the game for the game.



I'm curious about others here who work this way. If you're more director than programmer or artist, how do you keep the AI consistent on a big project, both the characters and the code? And how have you dealt with the backlash, if you've gotten any?



\*\*Play it free in your browser:\*\* [https://www.scuffletcg.com](https://www.scuffletcg.com)



Wiki: https://scuffletcg.fandom.com · Discord: https://discord.gg/yU3zZdE4aJ · Kickstarter (to pay real artists): https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/scuffletcg/scuffle-the-card-game-of-war-with-attitude

comments.author: Agile_Branch_8743
comments.body: I'm not giving you my e-mail to have a look at your game.

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body: Please don't require a sign-in. This is needless friction for something nobody is invested in. You don't even have a trailer. Just let the player play through the tutorial or a few rounds before requiring a sign-in. Give them something worthy of their investment in time - the biggest comodity in a world with tens of thousands of games coming out daily.

replies.author: ugotpauld
replies.body: Ive seen this so often that I have to imagine its an ai artifact where someone says "make me an online version" and it just defaults to accounts systems

replies.author: re-skob
replies.body: yeah, I don't know what's worse - the idea that this is basically one prompt where they just asked for an online card game and this is the default, or they actually went through several iterations of prompting to lock players behind this wall

comments.author: Mental_Tailor_4227
comments.body: Played it with a throw away email, don’t like it ….. the email part the art is actually pretty good, reminds me of an old TCG I use to play. The outer frame is too colorful for me what I would like to see as a TCG player is the combination of TCG……. Nm that just gave me an idea but yes 👍🏼 carry on my good sir

comments.author: theflossboss1
comments.body: This is by definition slop.  It just happens to be AI slop too which gives the rest of us a bad name

comments.body:
